sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 81 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: If only My people would listen
study.intro: Asaph calls Israel to a joyful festival, then God Himself speaks, recalling the rescue from Egypt and pleading with His people to listen so He can feed them with the finest wheat.
study.context: Psalm 81 is headed 'For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. Of Asaph.' It begins as a summons to celebrate a feast with music and the ram's horn, likely the Feast of Trumpets and Tabernacles in the seventh month. From verse 6 onward the voice shifts and God speaks directly, as in a prophetic sermon delivered at the festival. He recalls the Exodus and the waters of Meribah, restates the first commandment, grieves Israel's refusal to listen, and promises abundance if they would only follow Him.
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph, the Levite worship leader appointed by David; the app has no Asaph profile yet, so no person card is linked. The psalm names Jacob and Joseph and recalls the Exodus led by Moses, so Jacob and Moses are linked. Planned paintings would show festivals, wilderness scenes and harvest fields; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Joy to God our strength
verses.heading: A summons to glad worship
verses.meaning: The heading names the choirmaster, the musical term Gittith, and Asaph. Then comes the call: 'Sing for joy to God our strength; make a joyful noise to the God of Jacob.' Worship here is loud and glad, not timid. God is called 'our strength,' the source of the people's power, and 'the God of Jacob,' linking them to the patriarch whose God kept faith with a flawed man. Joy is commanded because God has given reasons for it.
verses.context: Gittith also heads Psalms 8 and 84 and may name a tune or instrument linked to Gath or to winepresses. Psalm 95:1 likewise says, 'Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD.' Exodus 15:2 sings, 'The LORD is my strength and my song.'
explore: Gittith
A musical term in some psalm headings, possibly an instrument or melody connected with Gath or with the grape harvest.
God of Jacob
A title reminding Israel that God bound Himself to their ancestor Jacob and his descendants by covenant.
verses.reflect: What reasons do you have today to make a joyful noise to God, even if your voice feels quiet?
verses.alt: A crowd of villagers in festival clothes raise their hands and sing on a hillside at dawn.

verses.title: Tambourine, harp and lyre
verses.heading: Every instrument joins in
verses.meaning: Verse 2 brings in the band: 'Lift up a song, strike the tambourine, play the sweet-sounding harp and lyre.' Percussion, strings and voices all take part. Israel's worship used skill and beauty, and it welcomed rhythm and dancing as well as gentle melody. The psalm treats music as a gift to be offered back to God. Nothing about this praise is half-hearted; it is a full, gathered celebration.
verses.context: Exodus 15:20 tells of Miriam taking a tambourine and leading the women in dance. 1 Chronicles 15:16 records David appointing Levites to play harps, lyres and cymbals. Psalm 150:3-4 calls for horn, harp, lyre and tambourine.
explore: Tambourine
A hand drum, often with jingles, played especially in joyful processions and dances.
Lyre
A stringed instrument with a wooden frame, plucked by hand; David was known as a skilled player.
verses.reflect: What gift or skill could you offer to God as an act of worship this week?
verses.alt: Musicians with hand drums and wooden lyres play beside a crowd under festival banners.

verses.title: Ram's horn at the New Moon
verses.heading: Marking sacred time
verses.meaning: Verse 3 sets the calendar: 'Sound the ram's horn at the New Moon, and at the full moon on the day of our Feast.' The shofar blast announced holy days. The new moon of the seventh month was the Feast of Trumpets, and the full moon two weeks later began the Feast of Tabernacles. God shaped Israel's year around remembering His acts. Sacred time trained His people to stop and rejoice together.
verses.context: Leviticus 23:24 commands a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts on the first day of the seventh month. Leviticus 23:34 begins the Feast of Tabernacles on the fifteenth day. Numbers 10:10 says trumpets were blown at the new moon feasts.
explore: Ram's horn
The shofar, a trumpet made from a ram's horn, blown to call assemblies and announce holy days.
New Moon
The start of each month in Israel's lunar calendar, marked with special offerings and gatherings.
verses.reflect: What rhythms in your week or year help you stop and remember what God has done?
verses.alt: A man blows a curved ram's horn on a hilltop as a thin new moon rises at dusk.

verses.title: A statute for Israel
verses.heading: Celebration by command
verses.meaning: Verse 4 explains why they celebrate: 'For this is a statute for Israel, an ordinance of the God of Jacob.' The festival is not a human invention or a mere tradition. God Himself ordered it. That makes joy an act of obedience. It also means the feast carries authority and meaning beyond any one generation's mood. God commands rejoicing because He knows His people need to remember and give thanks.
verses.context: Leviticus 23:41 calls the Feast of Tabernacles a permanent statute for the generations to come. Deuteronomy 16:15 says to celebrate for seven days 'and your joy will be complete.' Nehemiah 8:17 records Israel keeping the feast again with great joy.
explore: Statute
A fixed law or decree that remains in force, here a permanent instruction from God.
Ordinance
An authoritative rule or appointed practice, often concerning worship and sacred times.
verses.reflect: How might seeing joy and thanksgiving as something God asks of you change the way you approach worship?
verses.alt: Elders read from a scroll to families gathered under leafy shelters during a festival.

verses.title: An unfamiliar language
verses.heading: Remembering life in Egypt
verses.meaning: Verse 5 adds: 'He ordained it as a testimony for Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt, where I heard an unfamiliar language.' Joseph stands for the whole people. The feast testifies to what God did when He moved against Egypt. The speaker remembers hearing a strange tongue, a sign of being foreigners and slaves in another land. Some read it as hearing a voice not yet known, God's own, about to speak.
verses.context: Genesis 42:23 notes Joseph used an interpreter so his brothers would not know he understood them. Exodus 11:4 says the LORD would go out through Egypt at midnight. Deuteronomy 28:49 warns of a nation whose language you will not understand.
explore: Testimony
A lasting witness or reminder, here a festival that keeps telling what God did.
Joseph
Jacob's son, used here as a name for all Israel, whose family settled in Egypt during famine.
verses.reflect: What part of your past reminds you of a time God brought you out of a strange or hard place?
verses.alt: Weary laborers in plain tunics look up from brick-making beside a broad river.

verses.title: Freed from the basket
verses.heading: God lifts the burden
verses.meaning: In verse 6 God begins to speak: 'I relieved his shoulder of the burden; his hands were freed from the basket.' The picture is precise. Hebrew slaves carried clay and bricks in baskets on their shoulders. God took that load off. Salvation is described in physical terms: aching shoulders eased, hands set free. The Lord who rescued Israel cares about the weight people carry, not only their souls.
verses.context: Exodus 1:14 says the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar. Exodus 6:6 promises, 'I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians.' Matthew 11:28 invites all who are weary and burdened to come to Jesus for rest.
explore: Burden
A heavy load carried on the shoulder, here the forced labor of slavery in Egypt.
Basket
The carrying basket slaves used to haul clay and bricks, a symbol of their bondage.
verses.reflect: What burden would you like God to lift from your shoulders today?
verses.alt: An empty reed basket lies on the ground as freed workers walk away toward the open desert.

verses.title: Answered from the thunder
verses.heading: Rescue and testing
verses.meaning: Verse 7 continues: 'You called out in distress, and I rescued you; I answered you from the cloud of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah.' God heard Israel's groaning in Egypt and rescued them. He spoke from the thundercloud at Sinai. Then at Meribah, when they quarreled over water, He tested them. Grace came first; testing followed. 'Selah' invites the hearer to pause and let this history sink in.
verses.context: Exodus 2:23-24 says God heard the Israelites' groaning. Exodus 19:16 describes thunder, lightning and a thick cloud on the mountain. Exodus 17:7 explains that the place was called Massah and Meribah because Israel quarreled and tested the LORD.
explore: Meribah
A place name meaning 'quarreling,' where Israel complained about water and God provided it from a rock.
Selah
A Hebrew term in the psalms that probably marks a musical pause or moment for reflection.
verses.reflect: How has God answered you in a hard season, and how has He also tested your trust?
verses.alt: Dark thunderclouds gather over a rugged desert mountain as a camp waits below.

verses.title: If only you would listen
verses.heading: God's pleading warning
verses.meaning: Verse 8 shifts to appeal: 'Hear, O My people, and I will warn you: O Israel, if only you would listen to Me!' Here the Almighty sounds like a parent pleading with a child. The words echo the great command 'Hear, O Israel.' God does not shout threats first; He longs to be heard. The phrase 'if only' reveals His heart. He wants relationship and obedience that comes from listening.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 6:4 begins the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One.' Isaiah 48:18 laments, 'If only you had paid attention to My commandments.' Matthew 17:5 records the voice from the cloud saying of Jesus, 'Listen to Him!'
explore: Hear
In Hebrew thought, to hear means to listen with attention and respond with obedience.
Warn
To testify solemnly or admonish, here God bearing witness to His people about the path of life.
verses.reflect: What might God be asking you to slow down and really listen to right now?
verses.alt: A shepherd calls out across a valley as scattered sheep turn their heads toward him.

verses.title: No strange god
verses.heading: Loyalty to the one true God
verses.meaning: Verse 9 restates the heart of the covenant: 'There must be no strange god among you, nor shall you bow to a foreign god.' Israel lived surrounded by nations with many idols. God's demand was exclusive. A strange god is any rival given trust or worship. Today those rivals may be money, approval or comfort rather than statues. The command protects people from giving their hearts to what cannot save.
verses.context: Exodus 20:3 commands, 'You shall have no other gods before Me.' Deuteronomy 32:12 says the LORD alone led Israel, with no foreign god beside Him. 1 John 5:21 urges, 'Little children, keep yourselves from idols.'
explore: Strange god
A deity foreign to Israel's covenant; any rival object of worship or ultimate trust.
Bow
To bend low in worship and submission, an outward act showing allegiance of the heart.
verses.reflect: What 'strange god' tends to compete for your trust or attention?
verses.alt: Broken clay idol figures lie in the dust outside a village gate at evening.

verses.title: Open wide your mouth
verses.heading: The God who fills
verses.meaning: Verse 10 identifies the speaker: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt. Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.' These are the opening words of the Ten Commandments. Then comes a tender picture: like a baby bird opening its beak, Israel is invited to ask boldly. God is not stingy. The One who did the greater work of the Exodus will surely provide what His people need.
verses.contextTitle: I am the LORD your God
verses.context: Exodus 20:2 opens, 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.' Psalm 103:5 says He satisfies you with good things. John 6:35 records Jesus saying, 'I am the bread of life.'
explore: I am the LORD
God's self-introduction using His covenant name, grounding His commands in who He is and what He has done.
Open wide
A picture of eager, expectant receiving, like hungry young birds waiting to be fed.
verses.reflect: What would it mean for you to 'open wide your mouth' and ask God boldly for what you need?
verses.alt: Young birds in a nest stretch their open beaks upward toward a parent bird.

verses.title: Would not listen
verses.heading: The sad history of refusal
verses.meaning: Verse 11 turns to grief: 'But My people would not listen to Me, and Israel would not obey Me.' After all God's rescue and generosity, the response was deafness. 'My people' shows that God still claims them even as He laments. Their failure was not ignorance but unwillingness. The verse is honest about how human hearts can resist even the clearest kindness of God.
verses.context: Exodus 32:9 calls Israel a stiff-necked people after the golden calf. Jeremiah 7:24 says they did not listen or incline their ear but followed their own stubborn hearts. Hebrews 3:15 warns, 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.'
explore: My people
God's covenant name for Israel, showing belonging even when they turned away.
Obey
To submit to and follow; in Hebrew this verb pairs closely with willingness to listen.
verses.reflect: Where do you notice resistance in yourself to what you already know God wants?
verses.alt: A group of travelers turns their backs to a guide and walks down a different path.

verses.title: Given up to stubborn hearts
verses.heading: The judgment of getting your way
verses.meaning: Verse 12 describes the consequence: 'So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices.' God's judgment here is not lightning but permission. He let them have what they insisted on. Their own plans became their prison. This is one of Scripture's most sobering truths: sometimes the worst thing is to be left to ourselves. Yet even this aims to bring people back.
verses.context: Romans 1:24 says God gave them over to the desires of their hearts. Jeremiah 11:8 describes Israel walking in the stubbornness of their evil hearts. Proverbs 1:31 says the foolish will eat the fruit of their own way.
explore: Stubborn
Hard, unyielding and set on one's own course, refusing correction.
Devices
Plans or schemes; here the people's self-chosen counsel instead of God's guidance.
verses.reflect: Is there an area where you have been insisting on your own way, and what might it cost?
verses.alt: A lone traveler wanders off a clear road into a tangled, thorny field.

verses.title: Follow My ways
verses.heading: The door left open
verses.meaning: Verse 13 repeats the longing: 'If only My people would listen to Me, if Israel would follow My ways.' The sentence is unfinished on purpose, carrying into the next verse. God's 'if only' is an invitation still standing. Judgment is not His final word. To follow His ways is to walk the road He marks out, trusting that it leads somewhere good. The door to return remains open.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 5:33 says to walk in all the way the LORD has commanded so that you may live. Isaiah 30:21 promises a voice saying, 'This is the way; walk in it.' John 14:6 records Jesus saying, 'I am the way.'
explore: Ways
Patterns of life and conduct; God's ways are the paths of faithfulness and justice He reveals.
If only
An expression of deep longing, showing God's desire for His people's return and blessing.
verses.reflect: What is one step you could take this week to follow God's ways more closely?
verses.alt: A clear stone path winds up a green hillside toward a village at sunrise.

verses.title: Subdue their enemies
verses.heading: The protection they missed
verses.meaning: Verse 14 finishes the thought: 'how soon I would subdue their enemies and turn My hand against their foes!' The word 'soon' stands out. Israel's long troubles were not because God was weak or slow. Listening would have brought quick victory. God is eager to defend those who trust Him. The verse invites reflection on how much disobedience costs and how ready God is to act for His people.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 28:7 promises that the LORD will make enemies who rise against you flee seven ways. Leviticus 26:7-8 says five will chase a hundred. Romans 8:31 asks, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?'
explore: Subdue
To bring under control or humble, as an army is brought low in defeat.
Hand
A picture of God's power in action, turned here against those who oppose His people.
verses.reflect: Where do you need to trust that God is ready to act on your behalf?
verses.alt: An enemy army retreats over a distant ridge as a village gate stands safe.

verses.title: Feigned obedience
verses.heading: Enemies brought low
verses.meaning: Verse 15 continues the promise: 'Those who hate the LORD would feign obedience, and their doom would last forever.' The enemies of Israel are called those who hate the LORD, showing that opposition to His people is really opposition to Him. They would cringe and pretend submission. Their judgment would be final. God's justice does not leave rebellion unanswered, even when evil seems strong for a time.
verses.context: Psalm 18:44 says foreigners cower before the king. Psalm 66:3 tells God that His enemies cringe before Him because of His great power. Philippians 2:10 says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus.
explore: Feign
To pretend or fake; here enemies cringing in outward submission without true loyalty.
Doom
Their appointed time of judgment, which would endure without end.
verses.reflect: How does it comfort you that God's justice will finally deal with all evil?
verses.alt: Defeated soldiers kneel with lowered spears outside a fortified hill town.

verses.title: Honey from the rock
verses.heading: Abundance waiting for them
verses.meaning: Verse 16 closes with promise: 'But I would feed you the finest wheat; with honey from the rock I would satisfy you.' The God who once gave water from the rock now offers honey from it. The finest wheat means the best harvest. This is a picture of lavish, satisfying provision. The psalm ends not with scolding but with what God longs to give: the full feast of His goodness.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 32:13 says God nourished Israel with honey from the rock and oil from the flinty crag. Psalm 147:14 says He fills you with the finest wheat. John 6:51 records Jesus calling Himself the living bread from heaven.
explore: Finest wheat
Literally 'the fat of the wheat,' the richest and best grain of the harvest.
Honey from the rock
Wild honey from bees nesting in rock crevices, a picture of surprising sweetness in a hard land.
verses.reflect: What good gifts might God be longing to give you if you would listen and trust Him?
verses.alt: Golden wheat fields ripple below a rocky cliff where wild bees gather around a crevice.
